title: Blood transfusion in children: checks, observations and reactions
blurb: Check a paediatric red cell volume in mL, carry out safe bedside identification and observations, and respond correctly to a transfusion reaction.
question: Leo, 4, weighs 15 kg and is not bleeding. His Hb is 62 g/L and the team aims for 90 g/L. Using the BSH paediatric formula with a factor of 4, what volume of red cells is needed?

teach.body: A child's blood volume is small, so a whole adult 'unit' can be far too much. Formally, the British Society for Haematology (BSH 2016) says paediatric transfusions are prescribed in millilitres, calculated from weight and the rise in haemoglobin needed. Plain English: work out the mL for this child, check it is not more than 20 mL/kg, give it at a weight-based rate, and identify the child positively at every step.
teach.cite: BSH Guidelines on transfusion for fetuses, neonates and older children (2016)

head: Part
Value
rows: No more than 20 g/L above the threshold
teach.caption: Worked: (90 − 62) × 15 × 4 ÷ 10 = 168 mL for a 15 kg child (ceiling 300 mL).

items.label: complete red cells from leaving storage

teach.body: Most serious transfusion harm comes from the wrong blood reaching the wrong patient. Use positive patient identification at every stage and a structured bedside checklist: the child's identity band (name, date of birth, hospital number) must match the prescription and the compatibility label on the unit exactly. Young children cannot state their own name, so the band check carries the identification; a child with no band cannot be transfused until a band is replaced and checked.
teach.cite: BSH administration of blood components (2017); SHOT

steps.label: Baseline
steps.sub: Within 60 min before starting: P, BP, T, RR

steps.label: 15 minutes
steps.sub: After the start of each unit: P, BP, T, RR

steps.label: During
steps.sub: Visual checks; act on any change

teach.caption: Children may not say they feel unwell: watch for irritability, flushing, pallor or a change in behaviour.

teach.h: Grading a febrile or allergic reaction

rows.label: Action
values: May continue with treatment and close obs

teach.caption: Moderate and severe reactions are reported to MHRA (SABRE) and SHOT. Return implicated units to the lab.

items: Stop the transfusion temporarily and keep the venous access open.
Assess ABC and call for medical help.
Recheck the child's identity band against the unit's compatibility label.
Inspect the unit for clumps, discolouration or leaks.
Record observations and follow the doctor's plan; report if moderate or severe.

teach.note: Transfusion-associated circulatory overload (TACO) is a leading cause of serious transfusion harm (SHOT).

teach.text: 'One unit' is an adult prescription. For a child, a red cell prescription written as '1 unit' should be queried: BSH says paediatric transfusions are prescribed in mL. A full adult unit can exceed 20 mL/kg in a small child and cause overload.

teach.h: Scenario: Amir, 9 months, on the day unit
teach.body: Twenty minutes into his red cell transfusion, Amir becomes irritable and flushed. His temperature has risen from 37.0°C to 38.6°C, with normal breathing and blood pressure. Nurse Chloe stops the transfusion, keeps the cannula open, checks his band against the unit label and calls the doctor. This is a mild febrile reaction; the doctor decides whether to continue with treatment and close observation, and she records it.

items: Prescribe in mL: (desired − actual Hb) × weight × 4 ÷ 10; usually not over 20 mL/kg.
Red cells 5 mL/kg/h; finish within 4 hours of leaving storage.
No identity band, no transfusion: positive ID at every step.
Obs at baseline, 15 minutes into each unit, and within 60 minutes after.
Reaction: stop, keep IV open, ABC, check ID and unit, call for help; report moderate or severe.

summary: You can now calculate and sense-check a paediatric red cell volume and rate, and carry out positive identification and timed observations. You can also grade a febrile reaction and take the right first actions, including reporting.

A.q: Leo, 4, weighs 15 kg and is not bleeding. His Hb is 62 g/L and the team aims for 90 g/L. Using the BSH formula with a factor of 4, what volume is needed?
A.why: (90 − 62) × 15 × 4 ÷ 10 = 28 × 60 ÷ 10 = 168 mL, which is under the 20 mL/kg ceiling of 300 mL.

whyNot.0: 84 mL uses a factor of 2, below the BSH range of 3 to 5.
whyNot.1: 420 mL uses a factor of 10 instead of 4 and exceeds 20 mL/kg (300 mL).
whyNot.3: 252 mL uses a factor of 6, above the BSH range of 3 to 5.

A.q: Tom, 3, is about to start a red cell transfusion. At the bedside check the nurse finds he has pulled off his identity band. What should she do?
options: Ask his mother to confirm his name and start
Replace the band and check it before starting
Start, as the prescription chart has his details
Tape the old band to his bed and start
A.why: Positive identification at the bedside requires the identity band to match the unit label and prescription. A new band must be applied and checked before transfusion.

whyNot.0: Verbal confirmation by a parent does not replace the band check.
whyNot.2: The chart is not attached to the child and cannot confirm identity.
whyNot.3: A band on the bed is not attached to the child.

A.q: Ayesha, 5, weighs 18 kg and needs red cells. The prescription reads '1 unit'. What should the nurse do?
options: Give the full unit over 4 hours
Ask the prescriber to prescribe in mL
Give half the unit to be safe
A.why: BSH: paediatric transfusions are prescribed in mL calculated from weight and the Hb increment. '1 unit' should be queried.

whyNot.0: A full adult unit may exceed 20 mL/kg in an 18 kg child.
whyNot.2: The nurse cannot alter the volume; the prescriber must calculate it.
whyNot.3: Rate does not fix an unsafe volume, and paediatric rates are weight-based.

B.q: Sami, 8, weighs 24 kg and is prescribed 240 mL of red cells. What is the usual infusion rate under BSH paediatric guidance?
B.why: Red cells are usually given at 5 mL/kg/h: 5 × 24 = 120 mL/h, so 240 mL takes 2 hours.

whyNot.0: 240 mL/h is 10 mL/kg/h, double the usual red cell rate.
whyNot.1: 60 mL/h is 2.5 mL/kg/h, half the usual rate.
whyNot.3: 24 mL/h is 1 mL/kg/h and would take 10 hours, beyond the 4-hour limit.

B.q: Grace, 6, weighs 18 kg and is prescribed a top-up of 450 mL of red cells. She is not bleeding. What should the nurse do before starting?
options: Query it, as it exceeds 20 mL/kg
Split it into two 225 mL bags
B.why: BSH: check the top-up volume is not over 20 mL/kg. For 18 kg that is 360 mL; 450 mL (25 mL/kg) should be queried.

whyNot.0: Starting accepts a volume above the usual ceiling.
whyNot.2: Splitting does not reduce the total volume given.
whyNot.3: Diuretics do not replace a correct volume calculation.

B.q: Mia, 10, is stable on intensive care after an infection. She is not bleeding and has no cyanotic heart disease. Her Hb is 76 g/L. The team asks whether she needs a red cell transfusion. What threshold does BSH suggest?
B.why: BSH: in stable children without cyanotic heart disease, a red cell threshold of 70 g/L is suggested. At 76 g/L she does not meet it.

whyNot.1: 90 g/L is a typical post-transfusion target, not the threshold.
whyNot.2: 80 g/L is the adult acute coronary syndrome threshold (NG24).
whyNot.3: 100 g/L is well above the restrictive threshold.

C.q: Amir, 9 months, is 20 minutes into a red cell transfusion. He is irritable and flushed. His temperature has risen from 37.0°C to 38.6°C; breathing and BP are normal. What is the most appropriate first action?
options: Continue and recheck in an hour
Stop it, keep IV open, check ID and unit
Stop it and remove the cannula
C.why: First actions for a suspected reaction: stop the transfusion temporarily, keep venous access, assess ABC, check the band against the unit label, inspect the unit and call for help.

whyNot.0: Waiting an hour delays assessment of a possible serious reaction.
whyNot.1: Any decision to continue follows assessment, not before stopping and checking.
whyNot.3: Venous access must be kept for treatment.

C.q: During a platelet transfusion, Lucy, 7, develops rigors and her temperature rises from 37.2°C to 39.6°C. What should the nurse suspect and do?
options: Moderate reaction: stop and return the unit
Mild reaction: give antihistamine and continue
C.why: Temperature over 39°C, a rise over 2°C or rigors is a moderate reaction. Stop the transfusion, consider bacterial contamination or haemolysis, and return the unit to the lab. Report to SABRE and SHOT.

whyNot.0: Rigors and a rise over 2°C are moderate, not mild.
whyNot.2: Continuing is not appropriate for a moderate febrile reaction.
whyNot.3: Rigors and high fever are not an expected effect of transfusion.

C.q: Josh, 2, finished a red cell transfusion 3 hours ago. He now has increased work of breathing and crackles, and his SpO2 has fallen. What should the nurse consider?
options: Delayed haemolysis needing review in days
Expected fluid shift needing no action
C.why: Respiratory distress or pulmonary oedema during or up to 12 hours after transfusion suggests TACO, a serious reaction needing urgent medical review.

whyNot.0: Acute respiratory compromise within hours of transfusion points to overload, not a reaction emerging days later.
whyNot.1: An allergic reaction usually causes itch or rash; crackles and hypoxia suggest overload.
whyNot.3: New respiratory compromise after transfusion needs urgent medical review.

reteach.title: Measure, match, monitor
reteach.question: What makes a paediatric transfusion safe from prescription to finish?

blocks.body: Measure: the volume in mL from the formula, not over 20 mL/kg, at 5 mL/kg/h. Match: identity band, prescription and unit label agree exactly at the bedside. Monitor: obs before, at 15 minutes and after each unit; stop and check at the first sign of a reaction.

root.label: Fever during transfusion
root.sub: Stop, keep IV, check ID and unit

blocks.text: Stopping does not mean removing the cannula. Keep venous access open so fluids and drugs can be given.

explain.body: Volume (mL) = (desired Hb − actual Hb, in g/L) × weight (kg) × factor (use 4) ÷ 10. Then check it against 20 mL/kg.

test.q: Ben weighs 20 kg. His Hb is 65 g/L and the target is 85 g/L. Using a factor of 4, what volume is needed?

whyNot.2: 400 mL is the 20 mL/kg ceiling, not the calculated volume.

explain.body: Red cells usually at 5 mL/kg/h, usual maximum 150 mL/h, completed within 4 hours of leaving temperature-controlled storage. Platelets and FFP at 10–20 mL/kg/h.

test.q: What is the usual red cell rate for a 12 kg child?

whyNot.2: 150 mL/h is the usual maximum for larger children, not this child's rate.
whyNot.3: 240 mL/h is 20 mL/kg/h, a platelet or FFP rate.

explain.body: Baseline pulse, BP, temperature and respiratory rate within 60 minutes before starting; repeat them 15 minutes after the start of each unit and within 60 minutes of the end. Observe closely throughout.

test.q: When should observations be repeated after a transfusion starts?
options: At the end of the unit
test.why: Observations are repeated 15 minutes after the start of each unit, when severe reactions often show.

whyNot.1: Waiting an hour misses the key early check.
whyNot.2: Waiting until the end misses early reactions.
whyNot.3: The standard check is at 15 minutes, not 30.

explain.body: Infants under 1 year receive components produced to neonatal and infant specifications. Ask the lab rather than using standard adult components.

test.q: Ruby, 7 months, needs her first red cell transfusion. Which type of component should she receive?
options: A neonatal or infant specification unit
The oldest compatible unit in stock
Any compatible unit in the fridge
test.why: BSH: infants under 1 year receive components produced to neonatal and infant specifications.

whyNot.0: Standard adult components are not the specification for infants.
whyNot.2: Choosing by age of the unit is not the rule; the infant specification is.
whyNot.3: The component must meet the infant specification, not just be compatible.
